newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Afghan battle for Panjsher valley intensifies.
newsitem.headline: Afghan battle for Panjsher valley intensifies.

text.p: The black-turbaned warriors of Afghanistan's new rulers face growing resistance as they try to battle their way into the valley stronghold of former government army chief Ahmad Shah Masood, witnesses said on Monday.

The hardline Islamic Taleban militia launched an attack on the Panjsher valley north of Kabul on Saturday, capturing the two hills at the entrance to the narrow, rocky gorge that leads into it, and carefully inched their way further in on Sunday.

Taleban commanders said they planned to make another serious push on Monday into the winding gorge. The road has been blocked by at least three landslides caused by Masood's men planting dynamite along its sides.

The officers said they had taken 15 prisoners as their bearded fighters pushed into the gorge with multiple rocket launchers and tank fire covering their advance. They would not say what happened to the prisoners.
Long-time western Afghan watchers said their treatment of prisoners could have a major impact on the fighting.
"Word of what they have done to them will get back to the Panjsher and if they've shot them, as does happen sometimes in Afghanistan, then that will stiffen the resolve of Masood's men," said one.
Morale in the Panjsher, where Masood last week declared a state of emergency and ordered all non-combatants to leave, is generally thought to be shaky.
Masood withdrew rapidly from Kabul on September 27 and retreated into his Panjsher valley homeland as the Taleban took the capital after a lightning push.
Reporters who saw them shortly after their arrival said Masood's troops were demoralised, tired and hungry.

But Masood spent the days the Taleban gave him before launching an attack to reorganise his defences in the valley and the Afghan-watchers said he could probably hold most of it with winter only weeks away, if he could get his men to fight.
"If the Taleban have been kind to the prisoners, that word will get back to the Panjsher as well and maybe their job will be a little easier," said one.
Until late on Sunday, many Afghan-watchers said they thought the relatively light resistance to the Taleban push had suggested the Islamic militia had the upper hand.
But then Masood's men launched an intense rocket barrage on Taleban rear lines, sending its gunners and rocket launchers scurrying for cover.

The barrage was fairly accurate, suggesting that Masood still had spotters on the hillsides overlooking the village of Golbahar at the mouth of the gorge, near which the Taleban heavy military equipment was based.
Masood prevented the Soviet army from establishing control over the Panjsher during a series of assaults in the 1980s, when it backed the then-communist government in Kabul.

The Soviet army used carpet bombing, helicopter landings, Spetnaz commandos and dozens of tanks and destroyed many of the long valley's villages, but always had to retreat in the end, pushed out by guerrilla attacks that gave Masood a reputation as one of the best Afghan commanders of the era.

But Taleban officers, whose men have swept all before them to control about three-quarters of Afghanistan in the two years since their movement was born in religious schools in refugee camps in Pakistan two years ago, said they were sure of taking the valley.
"I cannot tell how long it will take but, inshallah (by the will of God), it will happen," said one.
"The Russians cared for their lives, which is why they never took the Panjsher," said an artillery officer. "We Taleban are Moslem people and are prepared and happy to die for God."
